extracted.intended_audience: writers, playwrights, critics, and general readers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical discussion about the Chekhov's gun principle: the narrative economy rule that elements introduced should be necessary and used later, plus its variations and critiques. Useful for writers editing plot and playwrights structuring scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chekhov's gun (narrative principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative principle emphasizing that every element in a story be necessary, while irrelevant elements should be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a gun is included in a story, there must be a reason for it, such as being fired at some later point. The principle—recorded in letters by Anton Chekhov—advises conservation of narrative elements and removal of irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce plot elements early whose significance appears later
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot element introduced early in a story whose significance to the plot does not become clear until later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contemporary 'plot twist' meaning is distinguished from Chekhov's original intent of mere narrative conservation; it describes deliberate early placement of elements that pay off later in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only present devices that will be utilized later
rubrics_metrics.description: Only depict devices/items/props that are used at some later point in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: James Bond films present gadgets at the beginning of a mission and typically each device serves a vital role later. Anti-pattern: showing a device or prop that never plays a role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't make promises you don't mean to keep (do not introduce unused loaded elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: "One must never place a loaded rifle on the stage if it isn't going to go off. It's wrong to make promises you don't mean to keep."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chekhov's quoted admonition warns against introducing striking or loaded elements that create expectations the narrative never fulfils; such unresolved promises frustrate audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove everything that has no relevance to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: "Remove everything that has no relevance to the story. If you say in the first act that there is a rifle hanging on the wall, in the second or third act it absolutely must go off. If it's not going to be fired, it shouldn't be hanging there."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editing rule: do not include props, details, or subplots that do not later contribute to action, character, or theme. Variations of this formulation appear in Chekhov's and contemporaries' remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that enforcing single-purpose details can make a story predictable
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning a single role for every detail makes a story predictable and can leave it 'colorless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique (Andrea Phillips): rigidly forcing every detail to have a single payoff can reduce texture and surprise; consider when multiplicity of meaning or incidental detail serves voice or realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of inconsequential details (counterpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsequential details can be valuable; readers will seek symbolism and significance, but such details need not always be functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ernest Hemingway mocked the principle and valued inconsequential details (example: his story 'Fifty Grand' introduces characters who are never mentioned again). Anti-pattern to strict application: removing all 'extraneous' detail can deny realism, atmosphere, or texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate non-use of introduced elements can be thematically meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: An introduced but unfired/unutilized element can intentionally reflect a theme (e.g., lacking or incomplete action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donald Rayfield notes Chekhov's own The Cherry Orchard contains two loaded firearms that are not fired; they contribute to thematic meaning rather than plot payoff. Use non-resolution deliberately and with thematic purpose, not accidentally.
